title: Looking after your mental health
keyIdea: Low days are normal and usually lift within days. A low mood that lasts two weeks or more, or worry that is hard to control and gets in the way of life, is the time to get support. Sleep of 8 to 10 hours, regular activity and talking things through protect your mental health, while alcohol, avoidance and lost sleep make it worse. Know your routes: GP, NHS 111, Samaritans on 116 123, a school or college counsellor, and 999 if a life is at risk.

kid: Everyone feels low or worried sometimes. After a setback, a low mood often lifts within a few days. That is a normal part of life, not an illness. Two common problems are anxiety and low mood. Anxiety is worry that is hard to stop, often with a racing heart, feeling tense or feeling on edge. Low mood or depression means feeling sad or empty, losing interest in things you used to enjoy, and feeling hopeless. Both can spoil sleep and focus, and many people have both.
The NHS says a low mood that lasts two weeks or more could be depression. That is the time to see a GP. Do not wait for months. Help works best early, and talking therapies can help a lot.

Daily habits help. Teens need 8 to 10 hours of sleep and about an hour of activity a day. Talking to someone and breaking big tasks into small steps help too. Alcohol, drugs and avoiding what scares you can feel good for a short time, but they make things worse later.

Know where to go. See a GP for problems that last. Call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option if you need help urgently. Call Samaritans free on 116 123 to talk at any time. Call 999 or go to A&E if a life is at risk.
adult: This topic helps older teens tell everyday ups and downs from problems that need support, know the signs of anxiety and depression, and know how to get help. The NHS line is clear: a low mood lasting two weeks or more could be a sign of depression and is a reason to see a GP.

The lab works through five skills. Learners drag along two mood diaries and count low days in a row, sort signs into anxiety, low mood or both, set sleep and activity into their healthy ranges, drain a stress bucket with coping that works while quick fixes refill it, and match situations to the GP, 111, Samaritans, 999 or a counsellor.

A common mistake is waiting for months in the hope that a lasting low mood will pass, or treating a few low days after a setback as an illness. Another is avoiding what causes anxiety; The NHS advises facing anxious situations bit by bit instead, which slowly reduces the fear. Many teens also use alcohol or late-night screens to cope, which worsen sleep and mood.

At home, ask how your teen is sleeping and whether they still enjoy things, since these change early. Agree together who they would talk to. From 16 in some areas and from 18 everywhere in England, they can refer themselves to NHS talking therapies.

familyTip: Ask your teen two simple questions now and then: how are you sleeping, and what have you enjoyed this week? A change in either that lasts two weeks is worth talking about together.

practice.prompt: Jo has felt low for {n} days since a bad result, but still enjoys seeing friends. What is this most likely to be?
choices: An everyday dip that should lift
Depression that needs a GP today
Something to never think about
practice.hint: How long has it lasted, and is Jo still enjoying things?
practice.explain: {n} days of low mood after a setback, with enjoyment still there, is an everyday dip. Two weeks or more would be the time to get support.

practice.prompt: Sam has had no enjoyment in anything for {n} weeks. What should Sam do?
choices: See a GP and tell someone they trust
Wait a few more months
Drink to take the edge off
practice.hint: What does the NHS say about a low mood that lasts two weeks or more?
practice.explain: {n} weeks of no enjoyment passes the two-week line, so it is time to see a GP. Alcohol makes low mood worse.

practice.prompt: Which sign points most to anxiety?
choices: Worry that is hard to stop, with a racing heart
Losing interest in things you enjoyed
Feeling hopeless about the future
practice.hint: Anxiety is about worry and a body on high alert.
practice.explain: Hard-to-stop worry and a racing heart point to anxiety. Losing interest and hopelessness point to low mood.

practice.prompt: How much sleep does a 17-year-old need each night?
choices: 8 to 10 hours
About 6 hours
12 to 14 hours
practice.hint: Teen sleep needs are more than an adult's but less than a toddler's.
practice.explain: Sleep experts recommend 8 to 10 hours a night for teenagers aged 13 to 18.

practice.prompt: You feel sick with worry before parties, so you plan to skip them all. What does the NHS advise?
choices: Do not avoid it: build up time there slowly
Avoid them: it keeps you calm
Only go if you have a drink first
practice.hint: Does avoiding a fear make it smaller or bigger over time?
practice.explain: Avoiding keeps anxiety going. Building up slowly, for example going for a short time first, reduces it.

pool.prompt: It is 2 am and you need to talk to someone, but nobody is in danger. Who can you call?
choices: Samaritans on 116 123, free at any time
999 straight away
Nobody until the morning
pool.hint: Which service is free and open 24 hours a day just to talk?
pool.explain: Samaritans answer 116 123 any time. 999 is for when a life is at risk.

pool.prompt: You do not feel you can keep yourself safe right now. What should you do?
choices: Call 999 or go to A&E
Book a GP appointment for next week
Wait and see how you feel tomorrow
pool.hint: Is this urgent, and is a life at risk?
pool.explain: The NHS says call 999 or go to A&E if you cannot keep yourself safe. You will not be wasting anyone's time.

pool.prompt: You need urgent mental health help today, but nobody is in danger. Where can you get advice?
choices: NHS 111, choosing the mental health option
Only from a friend
A social media post
pool.hint: Which NHS number is for urgent but not life-threatening problems?
pool.explain: Call 111 and choose the mental health option, or ask for an urgent GP appointment.

pool.prompt: Your stress bucket is nearly full. Which helps drain it for real?
choices: Talking it through and going for a walk
Drinking alcohol to relax
Scrolling in bed until 2 am
pool.hint: Which choice still helps tomorrow, not just tonight?
pool.explain: Talking and activity really reduce stress. Alcohol and lost sleep ease it briefly, then make it worse.

pool.prompt: Lee sleeps {n} hours a night on school days. Is that enough for a 16-year-old?
choices: No: teens need 8 to 10 hours
Yes: that is plenty
Yes, if Lee has a lie-in at the weekend
pool.hint: What is the healthy range for teens?
pool.explain: {n} hours is below the 8 to 10 hours teens need, and a weekend lie-in does not undo a week of short nights.

pool.prompt: Mia is active for {n} minutes a day on average. Is she meeting the guideline for her age?
choices: No: about 60 minutes a day is the aim
Yes: any activity counts as enough
Yes: the aim is 10 minutes a week
pool.hint: What daily average do UK guidelines set for young people?
pool.explain: {n} minutes is below the average of at least 60 minutes a day that the UK guidelines set for ages 5 to 18.

pool.prompt: Can anxiety and low mood happen at the same time?
choices: Yes: many people have both
No: you can only have one
Only in adults
pool.hint: Think back to the sign that fitted both bins.
pool.explain: Many people with depression also have anxiety. Sleep and focus problems show up in both.

pool.prompt: Which is a sign of low mood or depression, not just a bad day?
choices: No enjoyment in anything for weeks
Feeling fed up after losing a match
Being nervous before a test
pool.hint: Look for something that lasts and takes away enjoyment.
pool.explain: Losing enjoyment for weeks is a sign of depression. Feeling fed up after a loss or nervous before a test is normal.

visual.caption: Everyday ups and downs, or time to get support? Drag each one, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Nervous the night before a driving test
Sad for a few days after a pet died
Fed up after a row, better by the weekend
Low most days for three weeks
Worry so strong you stop going out

lab.caption: Flagship lab: read two mood diaries, sort signs of anxiety and low mood, set healthy sleep and activity, drain a stress bucket and find the right help.
